ai.definition: Magnetized Target Fusion (MTF) is an approach where a magnetized plasma fuel is compressed mechanically using pistons driving a liquid-metal liner. This compression brings the plasma to ignition conditions, generating heat and energy.
ai.howItWorks: Pistons within a chamber drive a cylindrical liquid-metal liner that surrounds a magnetized plasma target. As the liner compresses inward, it crushes the plasma, causing it to reach fusion temperatures briefly each cycle.
ai.problemSolved: MTF aims to address the challenges of traditional magnetic confinement fusion by offering a potentially cheaper and more compact reactor design compared to tokamaks or stellarators.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves precise machining of components for the pistons, liners, and plasma containment systems. High-temperature materials are required due to the intense heat involved.
ai.buildProcess: Components are fabricated using advanced manufacturing techniques such as precision casting and welding. Testing and integration of subsystems follow a modular approach to ensure reliability and safety.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the complexity of the mechanical compression system, high-temperature materials, and the need for robust plasma diagnostics and control systems.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: MTF is in the prototype stage with ongoing research and development. The technology has potential to enter early commercialization once key technical challenges are overcome.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for fusion reactors are still evolving, but safety standards will be critical due to the high-energy nature of the process.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving consistent plasma compression and maintaining plasma stability. Safety concerns revolve around managing high temperatures and potential radiation exposure.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain at this stage, dependent on successful scaling and commercialization. Initial investments are expected to be high but could lead to significant cost savings in the long term.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will focus on improving plasma compression efficiency, reducing costs, and enhancing safety protocols. Collaboration between academia and industry is key for advancing MTF technology.

glossary.def: A fusion approach where a magnetized plasma is compressed mechanically to achieve ignition conditions.
Mechanical device that drives the liquid-metal liner in MTF systems.
A cylindrical structure used in MTF to compress and contain the plasma target during fusion attempts.

subsystems.name: Plasma injector
subsystems.role: forms a compact, magnetised plasma ring and fires it into the reaction chamber.

subsystems.name: Compression driver
subsystems.role: delivers the mechanical blow that crushes the plasma in a few microseconds.

subsystems.name: Liquid-metal liner
subsystems.role: a rotating molten lead-lithium vortex that collapses inward and squeezes the plasma.

subsystems.name: Reaction chamber
subsystems.role: a steel vessel that holds the vacuum, the liner and the blast of each pulse.

subsystems.name: Heat and fuel recovery
subsystems.role: the liner absorbs the fusion neutrons, carrying off heat and breeding tritium from lithium.

subsystems.name: Diagnostics and control
subsystems.role: times each pulse and measures what the plasma actually did.

buildSteps.title: Form the magnetised plasma
buildSteps.detail: Gas is ionised in an injector and shaped by coils into a self-contained magnetised ring (a spheromak) that carries its own magnetic field.

buildSteps.title: Create the liquid-metal vortex
buildSteps.detail: Molten lead-lithium is spun inside the chamber so centrifugal force holds a cylindrical cavity open in the centre — the 'liner'.

buildSteps.title: Inject and trap the plasma
buildSteps.detail: The plasma ring is fired into the cavity, where the liquid metal wall and magnetic field keep it away from any solid surface.

buildSteps.title: Compress
buildSteps.detail: Pistons slam the outside of the chamber; the pressure wave collapses the cavity inward at tens to hundreds of metres per second, squeezing the plasma and its field together.

buildSteps.title: Heat to fusion conditions
buildSteps.detail: Compression heats the plasma nearly adiabatically toward roughly 10 keV (about 100 million °C), where deuterium and tritium nuclei begin to fuse.

buildSteps.title: Burn and absorb neutrons
buildSteps.detail: Fusion lasts microseconds. The neutrons are stopped in the surrounding liquid metal, depositing their energy there.

buildSteps.title: Extract heat and breed fuel
buildSteps.detail: The hot lead-lithium is pumped out to a heat exchanger, and lithium in the metal breeds tritium to refuel the machine.

buildSteps.title: Reset and repeat
buildSteps.detail: The pistons withdraw, the vortex reforms, and the cycle repeats several times a second — the engineering challenge is doing this reliably, thousands of times a day.

prerequisites.why: the plasma ring has to stay stable long enough to be compressed, which has been shown only at small scale.
industrial hydraulics and pneumatic rams already supply the energies and repeat rates needed, though not yet with fusion-grade timing.
molten-metal loops exist in fission and blanket research, but pumping and sealing lead-lithium at fusion temperature for years is unproven.
tritium is scarce and radioactive; a plant must make and capture its own fuel.
a pulse-repeating chamber takes neutron and thermal shock that no qualified material currently survives for a plant lifetime.

pathway.milestone: bench-scale experiments forming and compressing magnetised plasmas
pathway.unlocks: evidence that a liquid liner can compress a plasma without losing it.

pathway.milestone: integrated pulse experiments that produce measurable fusion neutrons
pathway.unlocks: validation of the whole cycle — form, inject, compress, breed, reset.

pathway.milestone: a single-machine pilot plant that recovers heat and shows net energy gain
pathway.unlocks: a credible cost case, since the design uses cheap pistons and liquid metal rather than expensive superconducting magnets.
factory-built fusion modules small enough to site near demand, if materials and tritium breeding are solved.
